title: Meeting Esau (Genesis 33)
hookLine: the brother he cheated runs and embraces him
last: I WILL NOT LET THEE GO.

lines: A NAME YOU DREAD ON YOUR PHONE.
cards: A name lights up on a phone: someone wronged years ago. A stomach can drop before a single word is read. Jacob has carried that dread for twenty years.
When he fled, his brother was planning to kill him. Now there's Esau on the horizon, with four hundred men.
Jacob has already sent wave after wave of gifts ahead, goats, sheep, camels, cattle, donkeys, hoping to soften him. He splits his family into groups. Then he limps out in front of all of them.

teach.b: First, the bowing. Jacob bows to the ground seven times as he nears his brother. The one who stole a blessing that said nations would bow to him now bows, again and again, to the brother he cheated.

In the Douay-Rheims: "Then Esau ran to meet his brother, and embraced him: and clasping him fast about the neck, and kissing him, wept." The wronged one moves first. No speech, no list of grievances, no condition.
Then the gifts. Jacob insists Esau keep the animals. Esau says, I have plenty, my brother; keep what is yours.

teach.h: YOUR FACE, LIKE THE FACE OF GOD.
teach.b: And Jacob says something startling: seeing your face is like seeing the face of God. The night before, he wrestled God and called the place Phanuel, the face of God. Now he sees that face again, in the brother he feared.
Last, the honesty. Genesis doesn't make it a fairy tale. Esau invites Jacob to travel with him; Jacob politely finds reasons to go his own way.

teach.h: A PEACE THAT'S NEW AND FRAGILE.
teach.b: The trust is new and fragile.
But the brothers are at peace, and years later they stand together to bury their father.

Some readers hear an echo in Luke's parable of the prodigal son: the father sees his son a long way off, runs, falls on his neck and kisses him. In both stories, the one with every right to stay away is the one who runs.

how: Catholics pray "forgive us our trespasses, as we forgive those who trespass against us" in every Our Father, and the Church teaches that being reconciled with others is bound up with being reconciled with God.

o: Esau's army coming to take revenge on Jacob
the wronged brother running first to embrace
the two brothers settling down side by side

games.q: what's inside the meeting — tap the pairs.

s: Jacob runs to Esau to apologize
Jacob bows seven times. it's Esau, the wronged brother, who runs.
Jacob says seeing Esau's face is like seeing the face of God
the morning after he named the river crossing Phanuel, the face of God.
after the meeting, the brothers travel and live together
Jacob politely goes his own way. the peace is real but new. later they bury their father together.

games.q: you're Esau. the brother who stole your blessing twenty years ago is limping toward you, bowing to the ground. you have four hundred men. what do you do?
o: make him finish bowing, then decide.
run to meet him, embrace him and weep.
take his gifts and send him away.
games.why: "Then Esau ran to meet his brother, and embraced him... and kissing him, wept." no speech, no conditions. the wronged one moves first.

practice: Think of someone you're at odds with, a sibling, an old friend, a neighbor, a coworker; it doesn't matter who started it.
Picture them on the horizon, notice your stomach and shoulders, then picture the smallest step toward them, a short message, a hello at the next family gathering, without needing to fix everything.
If you pray, ask for the courage to run.

wordCard.voice: Meeting Esau. Twenty years after the stolen blessing, the brother who was cheated runs to Jacob, embraces him and weeps.

orig.note: Hebrew: face. Jacob names the river crossing Phanuel, the face of God, and then sees God's face in Esau's.

carryVoice: Your line: he ran to meet him. Twenty years of dread, met with an embrace. Day three hundred fifty-nine.
